title: A giant limestone landscape in Vietnam and Laos began 400 million years ago
body: Phong Nha-Ke Bang and Hin Nam No straddle the Vietnam-Laos border. Their limestone formations began developing around 400 million years ago, and explorers have documented more than 220 km of caves and underground waterways.
takeaway: Some of the most extensive river routes in a region can be hidden beneath its surface.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Phong Nha-Ke Bang and Hin Nam No
visual: an underground river flowing from a vast limestone cave mouth

title: A vast protected wetland is a small fraction of Brazil's Pantanal
body: The Pantanal Conservation Area covers around 1,878 square kilometres, spread across four protected areas in western Brazil. UNESCO puts that at roughly 1.3% of the Brazilian Pantanal.
takeaway: The boundary on a protected-area map gives only a glimpse of the scale of the whole wetland.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Pantanal Conservation Area (2000)
visual: an aerial view of a shallow floodplain patterned with curving lakes

title: Jeju has lava caves lined with pale carbonate deposits
body: South Korea's Jeju Island has a network of lava tubes called Geomunoreum. Their dark lava walls contrast with coloured carbonate formations on the ceilings and floors.
takeaway: A cave can take shape in volcanic rock and later acquire mineral features more often associated with limestone caves.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Jeju Volcanic Island and Lava Tubes (2007)
visual: a wide dark lava tunnel with pale mineral formations along its roof
